text: Programs are countable but languages over an alphabet are not. What follows immediately?
choices: That every language has a grammar, since grammars are also countable.
That some programs cannot be written in any language, only described.
That the halting problem is decidable for the countable subset of programs.
Most languages have no recogniser at all, by counting alone, before any specific one is exhibited.
explanation: A program is a finite string over a finite alphabet, so they can be listed and numbered; the languages are all the *subsets* of a countably infinite set, and there are uncountably many. So there are more questions than programs. This is Chapter 33's counting technique with infinite sets — count what exists, count what the mechanism can produce, observe the second is smaller — and it tells you the impossible cases are the overwhelming majority while saying nothing about which.
